title: Introducing Cedar Blocks: end the build vs. buy debate
summary: Four open, composable layers for your GTM system: sales data, sales intelligence, agent tools, and the rep workspace.
body_markdown:
Today, we’re killing the build versus buy debate.


There are good reasons to build your own GTM software. You know your business better than a vendor does. You can iterate quickly, connect your internal data, and design a workflow around the way your team actually sells. As agents make building software easier, more teams will do exactly that.


The usual response from software companies is that internal tools are fragile, hard to maintain, or missing the polish of a mature product. Sometimes that’s true. It doesn’t make the advantages of building disappear.


Meanwhile, existing systems of record still want to be the place where your reps do everything. Your data lives inside their model. Your workflows fit their abstractions. And the moment you want to do something specific to your business, you start building around the edges.


We think the next generation of GTM software has to work differently. It has to be open enough for your agents to use its data and infrastructure, and flexible enough to use your internal data in its workflows.


Soon, there won’t be buying if you can’t build on it.


## The finished product, and the pieces to build your own


Think of Cedar as both a complete, assembled piece of furniture and the pieces you need to build your own.


You can use Cedar out of the box for complex mid-funnel sales work: preparing for meetings, drafting follow-ups, keeping deal context current, finding opportunities to revive pipeline, and helping reps execute the next step. You can also use the underlying pieces to build something specific to your team.


That choice extends through the product. You can work with the data underneath the agents, the sales knowledge they use, the tools they call, and the workspace where reps receive their work. You can keep the parts that are useful, configure the parts that need to be different, and connect systems you already own.


Today we’re introducing **Cedar Blocks: a set of open, composable layers for building GTM systems that you own end to end.**


You get the infrastructure, maintenance, support, and product of a team dedicated to building this, with the freedom to use as little or as much of it as you want. Your engineering effort can go into the workflows that distinguish your business, while Cedar handles the shared foundation beneath them.


The goal is specific: agents that can do real-time, enterprise-quality mid-funnel sales work, track their impact, and improve from the work they do. To get there, four problems need solving.


## 1. A unified data layer designed for sales


Some questions are easy to answer by querying a tool live. “Who do I need to follow up with from the last few weeks?” might only require recent emails, dates, and replies.


Now imagine a different request: **we’ve released a feature; find every relevant prospect and write a useful, personalized message to each one.**


The evidence may be buried in a meeting from six months ago. A prospect described a problem, your rep explained what the product could do, and the conversation stalled because one capability was missing. The CRM might just say “closed lost.” The important distinction lives in the conversation.


An agent could search every transcript again each time you ask. But doing that across a year of calls creates a lot of repeated work. It also leaves the agent to reconstruct which people, companies, meetings, and opportunities belong together before it can reason about what changed.


### Turn conversations into data you can query


Cedar connects customer interactions across sources such as email, meetings, Slack, LinkedIn, and your CRM, then organizes them around the relevant people, companies, and deals. The result is a timeline of what happened, with the original context still available.


On top of those events, Cedar extracts structured sales information: objections, pain points, questions, product gaps, competitive mentions, and other moments that matter to your process. An objection can be connected to who raised it, how the rep responded, and what happened next in the deal.


That gives an agent a much more useful starting point. It can narrow its search to deals with a particular product gap, inspect the underlying evidence, and decide whether a new release actually addresses the buyer’s concern. It can distinguish a feature someone casually asked about from a capability that prevented them from buying.


The same structure supports other questions. Which opportunities mentioned a competitor renewal? Which buyers asked for a capability you now offer? Which accounts have a change in timing that makes a previous conversation relevant again?


### Combine sales context with your own data


Your sales conversations are only part of the picture. Product usage, billing, support, and internal research may tell you something a sales tool cannot know on its own.


For example, you might want an upsell agent that combines a customer’s usage with the goals they described during the sales process. Usage tells you what they are doing; the conversation tells you what they were trying to accomplish. Together, they give you a stronger reason to reach out and a more specific conversation to have.


Cedar’s data can be queried, exported, and used by your own agents through its supported interfaces. You can bring your internal systems into the workflow instead of rebuilding every piece inside Cedar.


The advantage is a reusable foundation: connect and organize the context once, keep it current as new events arrive, and let multiple workflows use it. Each new agent can begin with sales data that already has structure and history.


## 2. An automatic sales intelligence layer


Access to data doesn’t automatically produce good sales judgment.


If you’ve asked an agent to do sales work, you’ve probably seen the result: a polished answer that could apply to almost any company. A generic follow-up. A plausible stakeholder list. A suggestion to “multi-thread” without a convincing explanation of who to involve or why.


In a complex deal, those details are the work. An agent needs to understand how your deals progress and what tends to help them move forward.


### Give agents a model of your sales process


Cedar organizes sales knowledge into a connected knowledge graph: the buyers and stakeholders involved, the problems they describe, the objections they raise, your positioning, and the ways deals develop over time.


This connects facts to one another. A pain point relates to a use case. A use case may matter to several stakeholders for different reasons. A product gap can explain why an opportunity stopped. A new capability can change what is possible for that same buyer months later.


Consider multithreading. Finding everyone with “VP” in their title gives you a list of people. Understanding the deal means asking who owns the problem, who controls the budget, who will evaluate the product, and whose involvement has mattered in similar opportunities. The useful output is a reasoned next step, grounded in your actual selling motion.


The knowledge also needs to change. Product documentation changes. Reps learn better ways to explain a feature. Buyers introduce new objections. A living sales intelligence layer can incorporate those changes into the context available to the next agent, instead of leaving each workflow dependent on an old prompt or a manually maintained document.


### What that looks like for Jon at Warp


In the launch video, Jon describes Cedar’s product knowledge adapting as his team updates its roadmap and explains new features to customers.


> “It truly learns. I was baffled a couple times.”


He explains that the useful context came from more than an updated document. It also came from previous emails and call recordings: how the team described the product, what it meant by a change, and how it introduced a feature.


His example is a prospect who asked about a product gap six months earlier. At the time, the answer was no. Later, Jon tells another customer that the capability is now available. Connecting those moments creates a reason to revisit the earlier opportunity.


That is the benefit of keeping product knowledge and deal history connected. The agent can use the new fact in the context of an old problem, then prepare a message that explains why the conversation is worth reopening.


## 3. Agent tools and superpowers, ready to use


Once an agent understands the deal, it needs a way to do the work.


Building an agent that identifies a missing stakeholder is one step. Researching that person, mapping the buying group, finding a relevant reason to reach out, preparing the message, and putting it in front of the rep requires a broader set of capabilities.


Cedar packages tools for that work: researching people and companies, building org charts, working with sales conversations and documents, following relevant external signals, and preparing outputs such as drafts, reports, and tasks.


### Build the workflow around the outcome


An org-mapping agent might begin with the stakeholders already involved in a deal, identify gaps in the buying group, research relevant people, and prepare a suggested introduction for the rep to review.


A revival agent might start with a product release or competitor renewal, find opportunities where that change matters, read the previous conversation, and prepare a specific follow-up.


A deal-risk agent might check for stalled progress, inspect what was promised, and prepare the next action with the evidence attached. The exact rules should come from your sales process and the signals you trust.


These workflows share useful capabilities. You shouldn’t have to recreate the connection to each system, the research workflow, or the output format every time you build another agent.


### Use Cedar’s agents, or bring your own


You can start with Cedar’s existing agents and configure their instructions and workflows. If you already have an agent running elsewhere, Cedar’s MCP interfaces let it work with Cedar context and supported outputs such as documents and tasks.


That means your preferred agent environment can stay in place. You can use Cedar for the sales context, tools, and delivery surfaces around it. Or you can run the workflow in Cedar and connect it to an external system where specialized work needs to happen.


The advantage is faster iteration on the part you actually care about: what the agent should accomplish, when it should run, which evidence it should consider, and what a useful result looks like. The common plumbing can be shared across workflows.


It also gives you something concrete to evaluate. Did the rep use the proposed action? Did the buyer respond? Did the opportunity progress? Connecting agent work to the underlying sales events gives you a basis for measuring outcomes and refining the workflow, rather than judging it only by how convincing its output sounds.


## 4. A rep workspace people will actually use


A lot of teams come to us with powerful agents and workflows already built. Their problem is that reps aren’t using them.


That problem is easy to underestimate. A workflow can be technically impressive and still lose to an existing habit. Reps have spent years working in Gmail, their CRM, and Slack. A new destination has to make the next action easier enough to earn its place in that routine.


Sending a notification that says “follow up with this account” leaves most of the work to the rep. They still have to find the conversation, reconstruct the context, work out what to say, and decide whether the suggestion makes sense.


### Deliver the work with the context


Cedar’s workspace brings the task, relevant deal context, and prepared output together. A follow-up can arrive with a draft. Meeting preparation can be available before the call. A suggested next step can sit beside the history that explains why it matters.


Reps can work through Cedar’s UI, receive useful work in Slack, or access context through their own assistants via MCP. The delivery surface can fit the workflow: a timely preparation brief in Slack, deeper account work in a deal view, or a queue of drafts to review and send.


For RevOps, that means the agent’s logic and the rep’s experience can be designed together. A playbook change can affect the work being prepared, the information surfaced alongside it, and where it appears in the rep’s day.


### Configure the workspace around your process


Different teams need different views of a deal. One might emphasize the buying group and missing decision makers. Another might need a mutual action plan, open technical questions, or the steps remaining before a pilot can begin.


Cedar gives you configurable deal views and managed task infrastructure so those differences can be reflected in the workspace. You can make the agent’s output useful in the place where the rep takes action, without building a separate interface for every workflow.


That is the final advantage of the four layers working together. The data gives you the history. Sales intelligence helps the agent interpret it. Tools let the agent prepare the work. The workspace gives the rep a practical way to review and execute it.


We’ll share more about the workspace in a separate launch. For Cedar Blocks, the point is that it is part of the system you can build with, alongside the data, intelligence, and tools.


## What we’ll build with it


Cedar Blocks lets you use a complete GTM product while retaining room to build the parts that should be specific to your company.


You can start with an existing agent, change how it works, bring in your own data, or use an external agent with Cedar underneath it. You can take one layer or use the whole system. The infrastructure and the finished product are available together.


Next, we’ll show a couple of agents built using these pieces, starting with practical workflows that turn existing sales context into action.
